questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Separation of powers as a design choice
questions.learningObjective: explain why the framers treated separation of powers as a chosen arrangement
questions.stem: Drafters of a new national constitution split lawmaking, enforcement, and adjudication among three branches. Which view best explains why they made that arrangement a deliberate choice?

options.text: Concentrating all three powers in one body invites abuse, so each branch is built to check the others
Separating the powers is the natural shape that every government takes whatever its designers intend
options.misconception: believes separation of powers is a natural fact rather than a chosen arrangement

options.text: The three powers reach different subjects, so they naturally call for offices held by different people
options.misconception: believes dividing government by subject matter is what produces the separation

options.text: A decision by a court should never be questioned or reviewed by any of the other branches
options.misconception: believes judicial decisions must be final and unreviewable by the coordinate branches

questions.explanation: The separation of powers is a design choice because the framers judged that power accumulated in one set of hands invites abuse, and so they assigned lawmaking to the legislature, enforcement to the executive, and judging to the courts, with each branch able to check the others. It is not a natural fact of governance: earlier charters in the same period had deliberately left those functions combined, and a constitution that put all three in one body would have produced a different system.
questions.hint: Ask what would happen to liberty if one body could make the law, enforce it, and judge it too.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: explain why the country has both a federal and a state court system
questions.stem: The national constitution creates one set of courts and each state constitution creates another. Which account best explains why the country has two court systems?

options.text: Each sovereign draws its courts from its own constitution to hear cases arising under its own authority
The federal courts handle criminal matters while the state courts handle civil matters only
options.misconception: believes the split between the systems is criminal work against civil work

options.text: State courts are advisory bodies whose decisions bind nobody and settle nothing
options.misconception: believes state courts merely advise rather than decide disputes

options.text: The systems are separate because a single national judiciary would exceed the powers delegated to the nation
options.misconception: believes a unified national judiciary is constitutionally forbidden

questions.explanation: In a federal system each level of government is a sovereign with its own constitution, and each constitution creates the courts for its own jurisdiction, so the state courts exist by state authority and the federal courts exist by national authority. The two are therefore not a single hierarchy with two branches, and a case has to be brought where the authority to hear it arises. Keeping them in parallel courts also lets each system apply the law of its own sovereign without waiting on the other.
questions.hint: Ask which constitution each court derives its power from, and from whose authority it derives it.

questions.topic: Trial and appellate courts by purpose
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a trial court from a court of appeals by the work each performs
questions.stem: A court's name can mislead, so the reliable test is the work the court was set up to do. Which contrast correctly separates a trial court from a court of appeals?

options.text: A trial court hears the evidence and applies the law, while an appeals court reviews that record for error
A trial court settles constitutional questions, while an appeals court settles only questions of statute
options.misconception: believes the two courts divide by constitutional questions against statutory ones

options.text: A trial court hears only criminal cases, while an appeals court hears only civil cases
options.misconception: believes the two courts divide by criminal cases against civil ones

options.text: A trial court is where a case begins, while an appeals court is where a case always ends for good
options.misconception: believes the defining difference is position in the sequence of a case

questions.explanation: The distinction is functional rather than nominal. A court of first instance hears witnesses, resolves disputes of fact, and applies the governing law; a court of appeals works from the record the first court produced and asks whether the law was applied correctly. Because the appellate court reviews an existing record rather than taking new evidence, it does not retry the case, and a trial court is a trial court whatever title its statute gives it.
questions.hint: Ask which court takes evidence and which court works only from a record already made.

questions.topic: What the constitution fixes about the Supreme Court
questions.learningObjective: distinguish what the constitutional text fixes about the highest court from what is set by law
questions.stem: A proposal would change the size of the nation's highest court. Which statement about how that court is constituted is accurate?

options.text: The constitution appoints the justices and fixes tenure during good behaviour, and the number is set by law
The constitution fixes both the number of justices and their tenure, so no law may alter either
options.misconception: believes the constitutional text itself fixes how many justices there are

options.text: The constitution fixes neither the number nor the tenure, leaving both entirely to ordinary legislation
options.misconception: believes the constitution leaves appointment and tenure to legislation

options.text: The constitution fixes the number of justices, while appointment and tenure are left to ordinary legislation
options.misconception: believes the constitutional text fixes the number but not the tenure

questions.explanation: Article III vests the judicial power in one Supreme Court, and the Appointments Clause provides that the judges hold their offices during good behaviour and are appointed by the president with the advice and consent of the Senate. The number of justices is set by statute rather than written into the constitutional text, which is why Congress can alter it, while good behaviour tenure is what insulates the Court from ordinary election turnover and the appointment clause deliberately places selection in two of the three branches.
questions.hint: Ask which features a legislature could change by ordinary law, and which it could not.

questions.topic: The establishing decision on judicial review
questions.learningObjective: identify the doctrine established when a court first refuses to apply an enacted law
questions.stem: A party to a lawsuit asks the Court to refuse to apply a statute the legislature has already passed, arguing that the statute is inconsistent with the constitution, and the Court agrees. Which doctrine is being established?

options.text: Judicial review, by which a court declares a law unconstitutional and declines to apply it
Judicial supremacy, by which a court appoints the officers of the other two branches
options.misconception: confuses judicial review with judicial supremacy

options.text: A private remedy, by which a judge issues orders against an opponent in a civil suit
options.misconception: confuses judicial review with an ordinary private-law remedy

options.text: Declaratory relief, by which a court fixes a construction for future disputes only
options.misconception: confuses judicial review with declaratory relief

questions.explanation: Judicial review is the power to declare a legislative or executive act unconstitutional and to refuse to apply it, and it entered the system through Marbury v. Madison, in which a party with a personal right to an office asked the Court to turn aside a statute Congress had passed. The trap is judicial supremacy, which is the distinct idea that a court's construction of the law is the last word, not the power to choose the members of the other branches.
questions.hint: Ask what the court was asked to do with a law that had already been enacted.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: state what the courts claim when they decide the meaning of a law
questions.stem: The legislative and executive branches dispute how a statute should be read, and a court decides the question in a case before it. Which statement describes the position the courts hold in that situation?

options.text: On the meaning of the law the court construes, the ruling is the final one the other branches must follow
The ruling settles only the parties in front of the court and binds no other branch at all
options.misconception: believes a decision binds nothing beyond the parties named in it

options.text: The ruling is a recommendation that either other branch may decline to follow it
options.misconception: believes a judicial construction is only advisory for the political branches

options.text: The ruling binds the other branches only after both chambers vote to concur in the opinion
options.misconception: believes a decision needs legislative concurrence to bind the other branches

questions.explanation: Judicial supremacy is the claim that where the courts are construing the law, their determination is the last word, so the other branches must conform to it rather than re-decide the question. It is not the same as judicial review, which is the power to test an act against the constitution, and it does not mean a ruling binds everyone everywhere, since the operative effect of a decision is ordinarily confined to the parties and the questions decided.
questions.hint: Distinguish the power to test a law against the constitution from the claim to have the last word on meaning.

questions.learningObjective: apply vertical stare decisis to a trial judge bound by a higher court
questions.stem: A district judge must decide a case on an issue the court of appeals in the same circuit has already settled, and the judge privately thinks that ruling was wrongly decided. What is the judge required to do?

options.text: Follow the binding ruling of the higher court within the same circuit
Follow the ruling only in a case where the appellate court relied on a different precedent
options.misconception: believes a circuit ruling binds only when it was reasoned the same way again

options.text: Decide the case freely, because district judges are not bound by intermediate appellate courts
options.misconception: believes intermediate appellate rulings do not bind district judges

options.text: Follow the ruling of the highest court but ignore the ruling of the circuit court
options.misconception: believes only the Supreme Court binds a lower court in the same case type

questions.explanation: Vertical stare decisis requires a lower court to follow a higher court's ruling within the same hierarchy, and a district judge is bound by the decisions of the court of appeals in that circuit, whether or not the judge agrees with them. The only higher authority that displaces the circuit's rule is the Supreme Court or a later decision of the circuit itself overrules it, and simple personal disagreement with the reasoning is not among the exceptions.
questions.hint: Name the version of stare decisis that runs down the hierarchy and binds lower courts to higher ones.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: apply horizontal stare decisis when panels of one court disagree
questions.stem: Two panels of the same intermediate appellate court have decided one issue differently in separate cases decided last year. Which rule resolves the conflict between those two decisions?

options.text: The later panel follows the earlier decision of its own circuit unless the earlier one is clearly erroneous
The panel whose judges have served longest decides which of the two rules the circuit follows
options.misconception: believes seniority of the individual judges selects the circuit's rule

options.text: The two panels may each keep their own rule until the whole court sits and resolves the conflict
options.misconception: believes conflicting panel rulings may stand side by side as equally binding

options.text: Whichever ruling was issued most recently governs, with no inquiry into error or seniority
options.misconception: believes a later ruling always displaces an earlier one on the same court

questions.explanation: Horizontal stare decisis binds a court to its own earlier decisions, so a later panel applies the first decision handed down in that circuit unless the first is clearly erroneous or has been overruled by a higher court. The rule is designed to make the circuit's law predictable, and it also disposes of the ordinary reason for doubt about panel authority: a decision speaks for the court, not merely for the judges who happened to sit on it.
questions.hint: Ask which way stare decisis runs when the later decision comes from the same court as the earlier one.

questions.topic: Duty of a lower court under precedent
questions.learningObjective: state what the doctrine of precedent requires of a lower court
questions.stem: A lower court faces a controlling decision of a higher court on the very question before it, and there is no workable reading of the case that avoids the decision. What is required of the lower court?

options.text: Apply the binding rule, and resolve the remaining questions within the boundaries the decision sets
Refuse to follow the decision and publish an opinion explaining why the decision was wrong
options.misconception: believes a lower court may decline to follow controlling higher-court authority

options.text: Hold the case and wait for the higher court to reconsider the rule on its own initiative
options.misconception: believes a lower court may suspend a case to await a higher reconsideration

options.text: Choose whichever competing line of authority in the jurisdiction the lower court prefers
options.misconception: believes a lower court may select among competing authorities at will

questions.explanation: The doctrine of precedent is what makes a decision a source of law rather than merely a result, and it requires a lower court to apply the holding of a controlling decision even if the lower court thinks the decision was wrongly decided, working out everything else inside the limits the holding imposes. Departure is possible where the decision has been overruled, where the rule is genuinely unsettled, or where a clearly established line of authority has since eroded, but disagreement alone is not a ground for it.
questions.hint: Ask what the lower court must do when the controlling decision is squarely on point and settled.

questions.learningObjective: describe the intermediate appellate tier and how it is organised
questions.stem: Between the district courts and the highest court sits an intermediate tier of federal appellate courts. Which description of that tier is accurate?

A single national appeals body drawn from the most senior district judges in the country
options.misconception: believes there is one national court of appeals made up of district judges

options.text: A travelling panel of judges that convenes in each district to hear that district's appeals
options.misconception: believes appellate judges rotate to hear appeals in every district

options.text: Specialist courts that may hear only claims brought against federal agencies
options.misconception: believes the courts of appeals are confined to suits against the government

An appeal from a district court goes to the circuit containing that district, and the tier is not a government-only forum, since private parties litigate in it every day.
questions.hint: Ask how many separate appellate circuits there are and how they are staffed.

questions.learningObjective: distinguish original from appellate jurisdiction across the federal tiers
questions.stem: A plaintiff files a claim in a federal district court, and in a different case a party wants a decision made there reviewed. Which pairing correctly states the two forms of federal jurisdiction involved?

options.text: Original jurisdiction in the district court, and appellate jurisdiction in the circuit court of appeals
Original jurisdiction in the court of appeals, and appellate jurisdiction in the district court
options.misconception: reverses which tier hears a case first and which reviews it afterwards

options.text: Original jurisdiction in the district court, and original jurisdiction in the circuit court
options.misconception: believes both the district court and the court of appeals hear cases in the first instance

options.text: Appellate jurisdiction in the district court, and original jurisdiction in the court of appeals
options.misconception: believes a district court reviews decisions made by another court

questions.explanation: Original jurisdiction is authority to hear a case in the first instance, which for most federal matters means a district court, and appellate jurisdiction is authority to review a decision already made, which means the court of appeals for the circuit containing that district. The federal district courts are courts of first instance for almost all of their business, so a pairing that gives them appellate authority over another court's ruling describes a structure the system does not have.
questions.hint: Ask which tier hears evidence first and which tier reviews a record after the fact.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: explain the reason the courts require a plaintiff to show standing
questions.stem: The federal courts decline to hear a dispute in which no party has a personal stake in the outcome, however earnest the disagreement may be. What is the reason for that requirement?

options.text: Deciding live controversies keeps the Court inside its power to resolve cases rather than to advise
Keeping the docket short ensures that the most important cases are reached more quickly
options.misconception: believes standing exists mainly to protect the courts' calendars

options.text: Requiring a personal stake ensures a constitutional question is decided once and never retried
options.misconception: believes standing creates a permanent bar against revisiting a question

options.text: Requiring a personal stake guarantees that the loser in any suit may always appeal the ruling
options.misconception: believes standing is the source of the right to appeal

questions.explanation: The requirement rests on the case-or-controversy limitation, which confines the judicial power to real disputes between parties with a concrete stake and forbids advisory opinions; standing is one of the ways that limitation is enforced. Docket speed, single-decision permanence, and a right of appeal are separate concerns, and some of them run the other way, since a narrow standing rule can add a step rather than save time. A plaintiff who can point to no actual and imminent injury cannot invoke the judicial power.
questions.hint: Ask what a court would be doing if it answered a question no injured party had asked it.

questions.learningObjective: apply ripeness to a challenge to a procedure not yet applied
questions.stem: A plaintiff challenges a written procedure that exists on the books but has never been used against the plaintiff, and the facts needed to judge it do not yet exist. How does ripeness apply?

options.text: The claim is not ripe, because the question is not yet fit for judicial decision
The claim is ripe, because a written procedure may be reviewed on its face at any time
options.misconception: believes a rule is reviewable as soon as its text exists

options.text: The claim is barred as moot, because no dispute presently exists between the parties
options.misconception: believes a dispute is moot because the conduct complained of has not happened yet

options.text: The claim is ripe as soon as it is filed, whatever the state of the administrative record
options.misconception: believes filing alone makes any claim fit for decision

questions.explanation: Ripeness is the readiness doctrine: a court will not decide a question until it is fit for judicial decision, and a challenge to a procedure that has not been applied to the plaintiff and whose consequences cannot yet be traced to developed facts is unripe. The objection is not that the controversy has ended, which is what mootness addresses, nor that the plaintiff lacks injury, which is what standing addresses; the difficulty is that the record needed to decide does not yet exist.
questions.hint: Ask whether the court could decide the question on a record it does not yet have.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: apply mootness when a change in law removes the conduct complained of
questions.stem: A plaintiff obtains an injunction against a practice of a state agency, and while the case is on appeal a new state law makes that practice lawful. What is the effect on the claim now?

options.text: It becomes moot, because there is no longer a live controversy about that practice
It proceeds to a judgment, because an injunction already entered must be reviewed on the merits
options.misconception: believes an entered injunction keeps a case alive after the controversy ends

options.text: It is remanded for a fresh trial, because the governing law changed during the appeal
options.misconception: believes a change in law automatically sends a case back for a new trial

options.text: It is dismissed for want of standing, because the conduct complained of has now stopped
options.misconception: confuses mootness with the requirement of standing

questions.explanation: Mootness asks whether the controversy has ceased, and a change in law that makes the conduct lawful removes the very dispute the case was about, so there is nothing left to decide. The entry of an injunction does not keep the case alive, because an appellate court reviews the controversy as it stands rather than giving an advisory opinion on what the law once was, and a court that finds no live controversy ordinarily vacates an order entered below.
questions.hint: Ask whether the court would still be granting anything if the case were decided today.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: apply the exhaustion requirement to a suit filed before agency review
questions.stem: A statute directs an agency to review an application and to issue a decision on it, and a disappointed applicant goes straight to court without ever asking the agency to decide. What obstacle does that create?

options.text: The party must exhaust the administrative remedies the statute provides before bringing suit
The court lacks jurisdiction, because only the agency may ever interpret the statute at all
options.misconception: believes statutory interpretation is reserved entirely to the agency

options.text: The claim is barred, because a decision takes legal effect only after the agency acts on it
options.misconception: confuses exhaustion with the rule that agency action must be final

options.text: The party must first obtain an agency ruling on any constitutional question raised
options.misconception: believes exhaustion applies to constitutional arguments in particular

questions.explanation: Exhaustion of administrative remedies requires a party to use the review procedure the statute gives the agency before suing, so that the agency gets the first chance to resolve the dispute from its own expertise and so that the court's record reflects that attempt. A plaintiff who sues without completing the administrative route is generally dismissed without prejudice, and the requirement is procedural, leaving open who may interpret the statute in the first place.
questions.hint: Ask what the statute expects the party to do before it comes to court.

questions.learningObjective: identify the political question doctrine and the ground on which it rests
questions.stem: A plaintiff sues over the way a state legislature apportioned the seats in its own chamber, and the court concludes that the question was committed to the legislature by the constitution and admits of no workable standard for decision. What is that conclusion called?

options.text: The political question doctrine, which withholds issues committed to another branch
The abstention doctrine, which requires a court to avoid all constitutional questions
options.misconception: confuses the political question doctrine with abstention

options.text: The standing doctrine, which bars a party who shows no personal injury in the suit
options.misconception: confuses the political question doctrine with the standing requirement

options.text: The exhaustion doctrine, which bars a suit filed before agency review is complete
options.misconception: confuses the political question doctrine with exhaustion

questions.explanation: The political question doctrine is a narrow ground of refusal that rests on separation of powers: a court declines to decide an issue the constitution commits to another branch, particularly where there is no judicially manageable standard by which the claim could be tested. It is not abstention, which is a general prudential practice about passing on difficult constitutional questions, and it is not a defect in the plaintiff or in the administrative process.
questions.hint: Ask whether the constitution gave this question to another branch and whether a court could apply a standard to it.

questions.learningObjective: identify the appellate court's function when an order exceeds what a statute allows
questions.stem: A trial court enters an order awarding an amount larger than the governing statute permits, and the losing party appeals. What is the appellate court's function on that point?

To retry the case and award whatever amount appears fairest to the parties

options.text: To leave the order alone, because trial judges have wide discretion over the amount awarded
options.misconception: believes the size of an award is always within trial court discretion

options.text: To refer the amount back to the legislature to appropriate the money the judgment requires
options.misconception: believes a court sends a judgment amount back to the legislature

questions.learningObjective: sequence a constitutional objection after an ordinary reading of the statute
questions.stem: A plaintiff argues that a federal statute is unconstitutional, while the government argues the case should be decided on the statute's ordinary meaning with no constitutional inquiry. How does a court ordinarily proceed?

options.text: It construes the statute first and reaches the constitutional question only if that reading leaves one
It decides the constitutional question first, because constitutional issues outrank all others
options.misconception: believes the constitutional question must be settled before the statute is construed

options.text: It avoids the constitutional question entirely whenever any statute is involved in the case
options.misconception: believes a statute in issue always bars any constitutional ruling

options.text: It decides whichever question the party raising the constitutional claim prefers to litigate
options.misconception: believes the claimant chooses which question the court reaches first

questions.learningObjective: explain why a remedy may be narrower than the one a party requests
questions.stem: A plaintiff asks a court to bar a practice entirely, and the court agrees the practice is unlawful but confines its order to the parties before it and to the time already covered. Is that order defective?

Yes, a court must grant the full relief requested once it has found a violation

options.text: Yes, a court may not impose any limit that the requesting party did not itself propose

questions.learningObjective: identify a consent decree and what it replaces in a civil case
questions.stem: Settling parties ask the court to approve their agreement and enter it as an order, and that agreement changes the defendant's practice while admitting no fault and paying no damages. What is the instrument the court enters?

options.text: A consent decree, which ends the dispute by agreement and removes the need to prove a claim
A summary judgment, which resolves the case on the pleadings without any trial
options.misconception: confuses a consent decree with a summary judgment

options.text: A per curiam opinion, which states the court's holding without a named author
options.misconception: confuses a consent decree with a per curiam opinion

options.text: A restraining order, which limits one party's conduct while the case continues
options.misconception: confuses a consent decree with a restraining order

questions.topic: Role of the intermediate appellate tier
questions.learningObjective: state why a second appellate tier exists between the courts of first instance and the highest court
questions.stem: Nearly every federal dispute ends somewhere between the court that heard the witnesses and the nation's highest court. What purpose does the tier in between serve?

options.text: It decides most appeals finally, leaving the highest court free to choose which cases to review
It routes every district court decision to one single body of appellate judges
options.misconception: believes all appeals converge on a single national appellate body

options.text: It corrects errors made by the highest court before its decisions take effect anywhere
options.misconception: believes the intermediate tier reviews the highest court's rulings

options.text: It gives every losing litigant a fresh trial whenever the first court decided wrongly
options.misconception: believes an appeal is a second opportunity to try the case

Sending every district court decision to a single national appellate body would multiply appellate capacity enormously, and a court of appeals reviews a record rather than hearing witnesses again, so an appeal is not a retrial. Every appellate body corrects errors, not only the highest one.

questions.learningObjective: identify mandamus and the conditions that make it available
questions.stem: A statute requires an officer to issue a permit within ten days of a complete application, the officer has declined to act, and no other proceeding would relieve the applicant quickly. Which remedy fits?

options.text: Mandamus, an order directing a public officer to perform a duty the law plainly requires
Certiorari, a writ commanding an officer to show why a decision should be reviewed
options.misconception: believes a writ compelling an act and a writ ordering a decision reviewed are the same

options.text: Habeas corpus, an order requiring a detained person to be brought before a court
options.misconception: believes a writ compelling an officer and a writ about a detained person are the same

options.text: Injunction, a command to a private party to cease conduct that is unlawful

questions.topic: Naming the form of stare decisis
questions.learningObjective: identify which earlier decision controls and name the form of stare decisis at work
questions.stem: Two panels of one circuit have decided the same issue differently, and a third case now comes before that circuit. First identify which earlier decision controls, then report the doctrine that produces that result.

options.text: The later decision controls, because the most recent statement of law always prevails
options.misconception: gives priority to recency rather than to the first decision

options.text: The earlier decision controls, under horizontal stare decisis within the same court
The earlier decision controls, under vertical stare decisis binding every lower court
options.misconception: misnames the horizontal form of stare decisis as the vertical one

options.text: Neither decision controls, because a fresh panel may always select new law for the circuit
options.misconception: denies that a court is bound by its own earlier decisions

questions.explanation: The controlling decision is the first one handed down, because a court is bound by its own earlier decisions in the same circuit, which is horizontal stare decisis rather than the vertical form that runs from a higher court down to a lower one. Recency is not a test, and a panel departs only by showing the earlier decision clearly erroneous or overruled by higher authority, not by preferring its own view of the rule.
questions.hint: Ask which way the rule of precedent runs when both decisions came from the same court.

Preemption, which rests on the Tenth Amendment reserving undelegated powers to the states
options.misconception: locates the source of preemption in the Tenth Amendment

options.text: Supremacy, which rests on the Tenth Amendment reserving undelegated powers to the states
options.misconception: names the wrong doctrine and the wrong constitutional source together

options.text: Preemption, which rests on the Necessary and Proper Clause authorising incidental powers
options.misconception: locates the source of preemption in the incidental powers clause

questions.explanation: The doctrine is preemption, and its constitutional source is the supremacy clause, which makes valid federal law the supreme law of the land and therefore controls where a valid state rule conflicts with it. The Tenth Amendment reserves powers to the states but cannot defeat valid federal law, the Necessary and Proper Clause is an implied-powers provision rather than a statement of priority, and preemption is the name for the result rather than for the clause itself.
questions.hint: Ask which clause says that a valid national law overrides a conflicting state law.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What separation of powers prevents and costs
questions.learningObjective: explain the purpose, the mechanism, and the cost of dividing the three branches
questions.stem: The framers divided lawmaking, enforcement, and judging among three branches and gave each the power to check the others. Explain what that design is meant to prevent, how the checking works, and what the arrangement costs.

answer.exemplar: The design exists to keep any single set of hands from making the law, enforcing it, and judging the result, because a body that does all three answers to nobody and can act on its own impulses. The checking works through specific powers: each branch has some say over what the others do, such as the ability of the legislature to refuse money, of the executive to review what is presented to it, and of the courts to refuse to apply a law they find inconsistent with the constitution. The cost is slowness and deadlock, because every stage requires agreement and a single objection can stop a programme, so the system trades efficiency for the protection of liberty against concentrated power.

questions.explanation: A strong answer names the danger of concentrated power, identifies at least one concrete checking power for each branch, and acknowledges the resulting risk of gridlock. An answer that lists the checks without saying what they protect, or that praises the design while ignoring the cost of deadlock, is missing half of what the question asks.
questions.hint: Answer in three parts: the danger, the mechanism, and the price.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Limits on the power of judicial review
questions.learningObjective: explain what judicial review may do and what it cannot do within the federal system
questions.stem: A court may declare a law unconstitutional and refuse to apply it, yet the same court cannot order the legislature to enact a replacement, and the legislature need not accept the ruling as a policy decision. Explain how both statements fit together.

answer.exemplar: Judicial review is a power to withhold the force of law, not a power to make law. A court decides whether an existing enactment is consistent with the constitution, and if it is not, the court refuses to apply it in the case before it, which leaves the legislature free to alter the law as it chooses, whether by narrowing it or by proposing a change through the amendment route. Because the court is confined to the case and controversy, it cannot order anyone to pass a law, cannot bind the other branches as a matter of policy, and cannot extend its ruling to disputes it has not heard, so its influence is real but its authority is bounded by what a case-or-controversy limitation allows.

questions.explanation: A strong answer distinguishes withholding the force of law from making law, and explains that the separation of powers plus the case-or-controversy limitation is what keeps a court from ordering legislation. An answer that says courts have the last word without noting that the result is only that the law cannot be enforced as written, or that omits the role of the case-or-controversy limitation, leaves a key part of the question open.
questions.hint: Distinguish a power to set a law aside from a power to write one, then say what confines a court's ruling.
